description: Year 12 physics student from coastal NSW, Australia, competing solo in the Universal event. I build instruments: a 24/7 aircraft tracking receiver studying atmospheric radio propagation, plus an automated cosmic ray cloud chamber in progress. For Earth System Trend Detective I'll use Python and AI to find reproducible trends in NASA Earth data. Solo by design; happy to swap notes on datasets.
summary:
TrendCheck is an interactive website that helps students and teachers investigate whether Australian climate trends hold up across datasets. We built a trend explorer that lets users choose a region, variable, and date range, visualize annual records, and compare rates of change and statistical uncertainty.

From 1981 to 2025, NASA POWER and Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology both showed national warming, at about 0.22 and 0.24 °C per decade, respectively. Both linear confidence intervals were above zero. The national rainfall records disagreed. In a guided Tasmania investigation, users predict what a third record will show, then reveal NASA’s IMERG satellite-and-gauge data and see how it changes the comparison.

TrendCheck gives learners a practical way to decide how much confidence to place in a climate claim. Users can download the data and follow the methods behind each result.
details:
TrendCheck is an interactive climate investigation for students, teachers, and anyone who wants to check whether a reported trend holds up across datasets. Users choose a region, variable, and date range, then compare annual time series, rates of change, and uncertainty. They can switch the national temperature map between estimated warming rates and the grid cells that pass a significance test after correction for multiple comparisons.

The guided investigation asks whether Tasmania got drier from 2000 to 2024. Users compare NASA POWER with Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology, make a prediction, and reveal NASA’s IMERG satellite-and-gauge rainfall record. All three records estimate a decline, but the size of the decline differs substantially. The Bureau’s and IMERG’s confidence intervals include zero. This is the project’s creative feature. Users make a judgment, add evidence, and decide whether to revise their conclusion.

We wrote the data processing and statistical analysis in Python and built the website with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We developed and tested it on a MacBook, used GitHub for version control, and deployed it on Porkbun Static Hosting. ChatGPT/Codex assisted with development and analysis code, and Roundtable supported advisory review. The charts and statistics were calculated from the cited data.

We considered how the choice of dataset, study period, location, and statistical method could affect the findings. We aligned the records over matched years, checked how coastal grid coverage affected estimates, kept Sen slopes distinct from the confidence intervals for separate linear fits, and tested how national rainfall uncertainty changed when we accounted for dependence between consecutive years.

The intended impact is to give teachers a classroom-ready investigation and help learners interpret climate claims for themselves. Plain-language definitions, chart summaries, and downloadable data let users follow the evidence and see where uncertainty remains.

NASA GPM IMERG Final V07 — monthly precipitation
NASA Terra MODIS MOD16A2GF v061 — evapotranspiration
NASA Worldview / GIBS — Terra MODIS true-colour imagery
NASA Earthdata CMR — live catalogue search
NASA Giovanni — local IMERG data extraction
NASA Hydrology Time Series Viewer — local GLDAS data extraction
projectRefs: Bureau of Meteorology ACORN-SAT — Australian temperature
Bureau of Meteorology AGCD — Australian rainfall
Bureau of Meteorology — Australian pan evaporation
Meteomatics Weather API / ECMWF ERA5 — local rainfall and evaporation
University of South Florida ERDDAP — NASA IMERG data access for the regional comparison
